1.grade_fit_note: politician is a common grade 4-5 spelling word; double-l and dropped-i errors are realistic.
1.note: Clean 2x2 design (l/ll x -ican/-ician); every option shares each feature with two others, so no majority elimination.

2.grade_fit_note: Languages vs. numbered course titles is a standard grade 5-6 capitalization contrast.
2.note: Spanish (a language) and Algebra I (a numbered course title) are both capitalized; 'math' correctly stays lowercase. B is the strongest distractor and is not defensible under mainstream guides.

3.grade_fit_note: Lowercase 'of' in document titles is typically mastered by grade 4-5.
3.note: Short prepositions stay lowercase in titles of historical documents. Correct, but light for grade 6.

4.grade_fit_note: Silent-e before -ment (developement) is a genuine grade 6 error.
4.note: A doubles both errors (ll and -ement) and looks implausible next to the others; otherwise a clean 2x2.

5.grade_fit_note: veterinarian is a familiar word; grade 6-7 is more typical than 8.
5.note: Distractors model the real dropped-syllable error (vet-ern-arian); sound item, slightly low for grade 8.

6.grade_fit_note: professional is a high-frequency word usually mastered by grade 5.
6.note: Clean factorial design, but D (both errors) is unlikely to attract a grade 6 student.

7.grade_fit_note: hazardous (-ous not -eous, single z) is reasonable at grade 7-8.
7.note: Sound item; -eous is a realistic analogy error (courteous, gorgeous).

8.grade_fit_note: restaurant is a classic grade 5-6 demon; the other sentences hold hygiene, guarantee, schedule as foils.
8.note: Good use of correctly spelled hard words in the foil sentences. The error sentence is noticeably the shortest.

9.grade_fit_note: suspicious with -cious is a fair grade 6 word.

10.grade_fit_note: conscious is often taught in grades 6-7; foils (nuisance, achievement, fiery) are appropriately hard.
10.note: Sound item. The error sentence is again the shortest of the four.

11.grade_fit_note: Knowing that short verbs and pronouns (Is, It) are capitalized in titles is a good grade 6 discriminator.
11.note: AP, Chicago and MLA all capitalize 'Is' and 'It' in titles; the 'short words stay lowercase' misconception makes B-D attractive.

12.grade_fit_note: mischief (i before e) fits grade 5; foils vacuum, receipt, pursue are solid.
12.note: Sound item. The error sentence is clearly the longest.

13.grade_fit_note: Period names (Middle Ages) vs. common adjectives (medieval) suits grade 6-7.
13.note: Chicago, AP and MLA lowercase 'medieval' and capitalize 'Middle Ages'. The only capitalization item whose key mixes one cap and one lowercase decision.

14.note: The -ize distractors are not accepted in either US or British spelling for this word (it is always -ise), so no second defensible answer.

15.grade_fit_note: acquitted (cq and doubled t) is a demanding grade 8 word.
15.note: Clean 2x2 (cq/q x t/tt); a good test of consonant doubling with final stress.

16.grade_fit_note: cemetery is a classic grade 6-7 demon.
16.note: Clean 2x2 of vowel choices; cemetary is a very attractive distractor.

17.note: The usual error (accidently) is not among the options, and accidentially is weaker than it; still a sound item.

18.grade_fit_note: Named wars and treaties are capitalized; standard grade 5-6 content.
18.note: A good foil is the second 'the war' staying lowercase, and every option keeps it lowercase.

19.grade_fit_note: Direction vs. region capitalization fits grade 6.
19.note: 'south' as a direction and 'eastern coast' as a description are lowercase; Midwest is a region. 'East Coast' would be capitalized, but 'eastern coast' is not, so A is not defensible.

20.note: Clean 2x2; D carries both errors and is weak.

21.grade_fit_note: accelerate (cc, single l) is a good grade 7 word.
21.note: Clean 2x2 (cc/c x l/ll); accellerate is very attractive.

22.grade_fit_note: questionnaire (double n) against liaison, fluorescent, perseverance is properly grade 8.
22.note: Strong item; every foil sentence holds a hard word that a student may suspect.

23.grade_fit_note: exaggerate is a typical grade 7 demon.
23.note: The misspelling 'exagerrate' moves the doubling rather than dropping it, a realistic error. Foils possession, discipline, colleague are solid.

24.grade_fit_note: Generic title (a senator) vs. named body (the Senate) is grade 6 content.
24.note: Lowercase senator and bill; Senate and Washington are capitalized in every option.

25.grade_fit_note: villain is borderline grade 5-6; foils circuit, biscuit are fair.
25.note: Sound item. D (ancient) holds a less tricky word than the others.

26.grade_fit_note: mortgage (silent t) is fair at grade 7-8.
26.note: C carries both errors and the odd -dge spelling; the silent-t omission (morgage) is the real distractor.

27.grade_fit_note: occurred (double r) is a classic grade 6-7 demon.
27.note: Strong foils (playwright, conscience, parliament). The error sentence is the longest.

28.grade_fit_note: The schwa vowels in permanent are typically mastered around grade 6.
28.note: Clean 2x2 of schwa vowels; a good item that sits slightly high for grade 5.

29.grade_fit_note: indispensable (-able, -dis-) is a demanding grade 8 word.
29.note: indispensible is listed only as a misspelling or rare variant in mainstream dictionaries and is not accepted as standard; clean 2x2.

30.grade_fit_note: comparison is usually mastered by grade 5-6.
30.note: comparision (from compare) is the realistic error; B (rr plus the extra i) is weak.

31.grade_fit_note: silhouette against conscientious, acquaintance, millennium is properly grade 8.
31.note: Strong item; every foil is a known demon.

32.grade_fit_note: Capitalizing the first word of each complete quoted sentence fits grade 5-6.
32.note: Both quotations are complete sentences after a dialogue tag, so both start with a capital. Slightly easy for grade 6, but acceptable.

33.grade_fit_note: foreign is a classic grade 5-6 exception to i-before-e.
33.note: Good foils (scissors, solemn, souvenir). The error sentence is the longest.

34.note: Clean 2x2 (a/i x -ice/-ise); sacrafice is the realistic distractor.

35.grade_fit_note: pronunciation (vs. pronounce) is a good grade 7 discriminator.
35.note: pronounciation is the key distractor. The -asion options are weaker but still plausible.

36.grade_fit_note: height is usually a grade 3-4 word.
36.note: D 'heighth' reflects a real spoken form, and some dictionaries list it as dialectal or nonstandard, not as an accepted spelling. C combines both errors and is weak.

_batch.Spelling: Fill-in items (1,4,5,6,7,9,14,15,16,17,20,21,26,28,29,30,34,35,36) are built as a 2x2 factorial of two error features. Every option shares each feature with exactly two others, so neither a majority vote nor a 'middle' option finds the key. Key positions are spread evenly (A5 B5 C5 D4), and the key is not consistently longest or shortest. The weakness is the double-error corner, which tends to be dead (4A, 6D, 20D, 26C, 30B, 36C) and is never the key; dropping it leaves three options. For find-the-error items (8,10,12,22,23,25,27,31,33), the foil sentences hold correctly spelled hard words, so a student cannot pick the item with the hard word. Length is the cross-item tell: the error sentence is the shortest in 8 and 10 and the longest in 12, 27 and 33. A student who picks the length outlier does better than chance on that set. Positions there (D,A,C,D,A,A,B,C,B) are fine.
_batch.Grammar and Usage: No items in this strand appear in the file (all 36 are Spelling or Capitalization), so no pattern can be assessed. The batch also has no Grammar and Usage coverage, though the diagnostic claims it.
_batch.Capitalization: All eight items (2,3,11,13,18,19,24,32) are a 2x2 of two capitalization decisions, with key positions C,B,A,B,A,D,C,D. That spread is fine, and no option sits between the others. The cross-item tell: in 7 of 8 items the key is a 'consistent' corner, where both decisions go the same way. It is both capitalized in 2, 11, 18 and 32 and both lowercase in 3, 19 and 24. Only 13 has a mixed key (lowercase medieval, capital Ages). A test-wise student who discards the two mixed options is left with 2 choices on 7 of 8 items, and is right half the time with no knowledge of the rules. Splitting all-caps from all-lowercase keys (4 vs 3) is balanced, so the tell stops at 50% rather than giving the answer. More items should have mixed keys.
